title: A World In Disequilibrium: The US, Germany And France
gist: Paywalled teaser of a Gavekal series arguing markets are still mispricing hidden disequilibria despite this week's bond moves, opening with Maurice Allais's rule that long rates revert to structural growth rates, applied to the US, Germany and France.

insights.claim: Despite this week's bond market moves, investors are still behaving as if markets are in a normal equilibrium state, when in fact a hidden risk (described as a 'great white shark lurking under the surface') has persisted for some time.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Investors treating current market conditions as normal may be underpricing a latent risk that has not resolved despite recent volatility in bonds.
insights.quote: We have not been there for quite a while, and the great white shark is still lurking under the surface.
insights.locator: Notwithstanding this week's bond market moves, investors are acting as if we are still in a normal world

insights.claim: French economist Maurice Allais's 'golden rule' holds that, over the long term, long-term interest rates always revert toward an economy's structural growth rate, implying persistent gaps between the two are unsustainable.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: A widening or persistent gap between long rates and structural growth (as plotted for the US) flags a disequilibrium likely to correct via rates, growth, or both.
insights.quote: The golden rule of French economist Maurice Allais stipulates that, over the long term, long rates (the blue line) always return towards the structural growth rate of the economy (the red line).

insights.claim: The author plans a series of papers examining disequilibria in long-term interest rates in the United States, Germany, and France as the starting point for a broader analysis.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Signals that US, German, and French long-rate/growth-rate gaps are the specific disequilibria to watch next in this research thread.
insights.quote: In my next few papers, I intend to look at some of the disequilibria that still exist, starting with long rates in the US, Germany and France.
insights.locator: In my next few papers, I intend to look at some of the disequilibria
